problems.title: Coil spring: torsion in the wire, compliance from the coil
problems.setup: A steel helical spring for a lunar lander leg damper is wound from round wire of diameter d = 4 mm to a mean coil diameter D = 40 mm, with n = 10 active coils. G = 80 GPa and E = 200 GPa. An axial load P compresses the spring along its axis. Treat it as close coiled (small helix angle) and use the wire strain energy only, neglecting direct shear.

parts.ask: Cut the wire anywhere along a coil. Which internal load dominates the wire cross-section?
parts.a: A torque T = PD/2 about the wire axis
w: A bending moment M = PD/2 about a cross-section axis of the wire
An axial force P along the wire
A torque T = PD about the wire axis
sol: P acts on the spring axis, a lever arm D/2 from the wire centreline
That arm twists the wire: T = PD/2, plus a small direct shear force P

parts.ask: Axial stiffness k of the spring by Castigliano's second theorem
sol: U = T²L_w/(2GJ) with T = PD/2, L_w = πDn, J = πd⁴/32
δ = ∂U/∂P = 8PD³n/(Gd⁴)

parts.ask: Straighten the same wire into a bar of length L_w = πDn and load it axially. Ratio of the bar stiffness to the coil stiffness
sol: k_bar/k = 2000/4 = 500: the coil is a compliance amplifier

parts.ask: Peak torsional shear stress in the wire at P = 100 N
Twist: the same coil now serves as a hinge return spring, loaded by a moment M about the coil axis. Its angular stiffness k_θ
sol: The moment vector lies along the coil axis, so it bends the wire in the plane of each turn, with M uniform along the wire
U = M²L_w/(2EI) with I = πd⁴/64, so θ = ML_w/(EI)

problems.x: An axially loaded coil puts its wire in torsion, a moment loaded coil puts its wire in bending, and the long wire makes either one a compliance amplifier.

problems.title: Rope held beam: when is the section all in compression?
problems.setup: A rectangular timber gangway beam, b = 100 mm wide and h = 300 mm deep, is L = 2 m long. It is pinned to a wall at A. Its free end B is held by a rope that runs back up to the wall at angle α above the beam axis. The beam carries a uniform downward load w = 6 kN/m. Neglect self weight; the pin and the rope act on the beam centroid line.

parts.ask: Rope tension T for α = 30°
sol: Moments about A: T sin α·L = wL²/2

parts.ask: Normal stress at the bottom fibre at midspan for α = 30° (tension positive)
sol: Axial compression N = T cos α = 10.39 kN, uniform along the beam
Vertical reactions are wL/2 at each end, so midspan M = wL²/8 = 3 kN·m
A = 30,000 mm², S = bh²/6 = 1.5×10⁶ mm³
σ_bottom = −N/A + M/S = −0.346 + 2.000 = 1.654 MPa (tension)

parts.ask: Largest α that keeps the whole beam in compression
sol: Midspan has the largest M and N is uniform, so midspan governs
Need N/A ≥ M/S with N = wL/(2 tan α)
wL/(2 tan α·bh) ≥ (wL²/8)·6/(bh²) gives tan α ≤ 2h/(3L) = 0.1
α ≤ 5.71°: the neutral axis then sits exactly at the bottom fibre

parts.ask: Rope tension at that angle
sol: T = wL/(2 sin α) = 12/(2·0.0995) = 60.3 kN, five times the 30° value

parts.ask: Twist: a gust now lifts the beam with a net upward load. What carries it?
parts.a: Nothing at B: the rope goes slack, the beam swings on its pin, and a strut or down-haul is needed
w: The rope, now pushing with a compressive force wL/(2 sin α)
The pin at A, which now acts as a clamp
The beam's bending stiffness, with the rope still taut
sol: A rope carries tension only
Under net uplift it goes slack, leaving a beam on a single pin: a mechanism
Add a member that can take compression, or a second rope from below

problems.x: Axial compression from an inclined rope shifts the neutral axis, and tan α = 2h/(3L) places it exactly at the bottom fibre.

problems.title: Hollow axle sized by Bredt: the thin wall trap
problems.setup: A titanium drive axle for a lunar rover is a round tube whose wall midline is fixed at diameter D = 40 mm (it is sized to a bearing sleeve). It must carry a torque T = 5 kN·m with an allowable shear stress τ_allow = 200 MPa. Start from the thin walled (Bredt) result τ = T/(2A_m t) with A_m = πD²/4.

parts.ask: Required wall thickness from the thin wall formula
sol: t = T/(2A_m τ_allow) = 2T/(πD²τ_allow)

parts.ask: What do you say at the board once you have this t?
parts.a: t ≈ D/4, so t/R_m ≈ 0.5 and the thin wall assumption is violated; redo it with the exact tube formula
w: t ≈ 10 mm is a sensible wall, so box the answer
A thick tube makes Bredt conservative, so the answer stands
Switch to the open section result τ = 3T/(2πR_m t²)
sol: Bredt assumes the shear stress is uniform through the wall, which needs t much smaller than R_m
Here t/R_m = 9.95/20 ≈ 0.5: the answer contradicts the opening assumption
Say so out loud, then use τ_max = T r_o/J

parts.ask: Exact peak shear stress in the tube with t = 9.95 mm (r_o = 24.97 mm, r_i = 15.03 mm)
sol: J = π(r_o⁴ − r_i⁴)/2 = 5.31×10⁵ mm⁴
18% above the allowable: the thin wall answer is unconservative here

parts.ask: Wall thickness that meets τ_allow with the exact formula (midline still at D = 40 mm)
sol: Iterating gives t = 11.85 mm
Shear peaks at the outer surface, so the outer fibre governs

parts.ask: Twist: the axle is remade in a brittle ceramic. Where does a torsion crack run?
parts.a: Along a 45° helix, normal to the principal tensile stress
w: On a plane normal to the axis, where the shear stress peaks
Along a longitudinal plane through the axis
On a 45° plane of maximum shear stress
sol: Pure shear τ has principal stresses ±τ on planes at 45° to the axis
A brittle material fails in tension, so the crack follows a 45° helix (like twisted chalk)

problems.x: Check t/R after sizing a tube, and switch to τ_max = T r_o/J once the wall is a sizeable fraction of the radius.

problems.title: L frame on two springs: asymmetric bifurcation
problems.setup: A rigid L frame has a vertical leg of height H = 1 m, pinned at its base O with a rotational spring C = 20 kN·m/rad, and a horizontal arm of length a = 0.5 m fixed to the top corner. A vertical linear spring k = 40 kN/m supports the arm tip from below and stays vertical (its lower end rides on a roller). A vertical dead load P acts at the top corner. The frame rotates rigidly by θ, measured from vertical, positive when the leg leans toward the arm.

parts.ask: Total potential energy Π(θ):
parts.a: Π = ½Cθ² + ½k[a sin θ + H(1 − cos θ)]² − PH(1 − cos θ)
w: Π = ½Cθ² + ½k(a sin θ)² − PH(1 − cos θ)
Π = ½Cθ² + ½k[a sin θ + H(1 − cos θ)]² + PH(1 − cos θ)
Π = ½Cθ² + ½k[a sin θ + H(1 − cos θ)]² − PH sin θ
sol: The corner drops H(1 − cos θ), so the dead load term is −PH(1 − cos θ)
The arm tip drops a sin θ from the arm rotation plus H(1 − cos θ) from the corner
Both shorten the spring

parts.ask: Critical load P_cr
sol: Expand: Π ≈ ½(C + ka² − PH)θ² + ½kaHθ³ + …
d²Π/dθ² = 0 at θ = 0 gives P_cr = (C + ka²)/H

parts.ask: At P = P_cr the second derivative of Π vanishes on the trivial path. What decides stability, and what kind of critical point is this?
parts.a: d³Π/dθ³ = 3kaH, which is nonzero, so P_cr is unstable: an asymmetric bifurcation, imperfection sensitive
w: d²Π/dθ² = 0 means neutral equilibrium, so the frame is stable at P_cr
The θ⁴ term decides, giving a stable symmetric bifurcation
dP/dθ = 0 on the path, so it is a limit point with snap-through
sol: When the quadratic term vanishes, the second order test is inconclusive: go to the first nonzero higher term
A nonzero cubic term makes Π fall on one side of θ = 0
The post-buckling path rises for θ > 0 and falls for θ < 0

parts.ask: Initial slope dP/dθ of the post-buckling path at P_cr
sol: dΠ/dθ ≈ (C + ka² − PH)θ + (3/2)kaHθ² = 0 on the buckled path
P ≈ P_cr + (3/2)kaθ
dP/dθ = 1.5·40·0.5 = 30 kN/rad: load rises for θ > 0 and falls for θ < 0

parts.ask: Twist: add an identical arm and spring k on the other side, making a symmetric T frame (P_cr becomes 40 kN). Writing P ≈ P_cr + Bθ², find B
sol: The two cubic terms cancel
Π ≈ ½(C + 2ka² − PH)θ² + [k(H²/4 − a²/3) + PH/24]θ⁴
P = P_cr + (4/H)[k(H²/4 − a²/3) + P_crH/24]θ²
B = 4(6.667 + 1.667) = 33.3 kN/rad², positive: stable symmetric

problems.x: A nonzero cubic term in Π makes a bifurcation asymmetric and imperfection sensitive, and a symmetric layout cancels it so the θ⁴ term sets the post-buckling path.

problems.title: Bistable latch: snap-through at a limit point
problems.setup: A bistable latch on a deployable boom is a shallow two bar (von Mises) truss. Two identical pin ended bars, each of initial length L₀ = 1 m and axial stiffness EA = 20 MN, meet at an apex with initial rise h₀ = 0.1 m. A downward load P acts at the apex under load control. h is the current rise and the apex drop is w = h₀ − h. Use the shallow truss approximation.

parts.ask: With bar shortening (L₀ − L)/L₀ ≈ (h₀² − h²)/(2L₀²), which load relation holds?
w: P = (EA/L₀³)·h₀(h₀² − h²)
P = (EA/(2L₀³))·h(h₀² − h²)
P = (EA/L₀)·(h₀ − h)
sol: Bar force N = EA(h₀² − h²)/(2L₀²) in compression
Vertical equilibrium at the apex: P = 2N(h/L₀)
P = EA h(h₀² − h²)/L₀³

parts.ask: Limit load P_max
sol: dP/dh = (EA/L₀³)(h₀² − 3h²) = 0 gives h = h₀/√3
P_max = 7.70 kN

parts.ask: Apex drop w at the limit point
P is raised just past P_max under load control. What happens, and how does it differ from a bifurcation?
parts.a: The apex snaps dynamically to the inverted shape; a limit point lies on a single path where dP/dw = 0, with no second branch
w: The truss moves onto a second equilibrium branch that crosses the first at P_max
The apex stops moving because the tangent stiffness is zero
The bars yield and the load stays at P_max as w grows
sol: At the limit point the tangent stiffness dP/dw falls to zero on the one equilibrium path
Beyond it the nearest equilibrium is the far branch (h < 0), so the apex jumps
A bifurcation has a second path crossing the first at P_cr
Displacement control would trace the falling part of the curve

parts.ask: Twist: each bar is a slender rod with EI = 160 N·m², pinned at both ends. At what apex load do the bars reach their Euler load?
sol: P_E = π²EI/L₀² = 1579 N
N = P_E when h² = h₀² − 2L₀²P_E/EA, so h = 0.09921 m
P = 2P_E h/L₀ = 313 N, far below 7.70 kN
The bars buckle (a bifurcation) long before the snap, so the latch needs stockier bars

problems.x: A shallow truss under load control snaps through at its limit point, where dP/dw reaches zero, and member buckling must be checked before that point.

problems.title: Propped beam with a flexible root joint
problems.setup: A floor beam in a surface habitat spans L = 4 m. At A it is bolted to a bulkhead whose joint rotates under moment: model it as a rotational spring k_θ = 3 MN·m/rad with zero deflection at A. At B it rests on a rigid prop. EI = 4 MN·m², and the beam carries a uniform downward load w = 4 kN/m. Take the prop reaction R as the redundant.

parts.ask: Boundary conditions at the joint A:
parts.a: Zero deflection, and root moment equal to k_θ times the root rotation
w: Zero deflection and zero rotation
Zero deflection and zero moment
Zero rotation, and root shear equal to k_θ times the deflection
sol: The bolts hold A in place, so w(0) = 0
The joint rotates in proportion to the moment it carries: M_A = k_θθ_A
Clamped (k_θ → ∞) and pinned (k_θ → 0) are the two limits

parts.ask: Prop reaction R
sol: Release the prop: a cantilever on a root spring under w and an upward tip force R
Tip deflection from w: wL⁴/(8EI) + (wL²/2)L/k_θ = 0.0320 + 0.0427 = 0.0747 m
Tip flexibility for R: L³/(3EI) + L²/k_θ = 1.067×10⁻⁵ m/N

parts.ask: Root moment M_A (hogging positive)
sol: M_A = wL²/2 − RL
M_A = 32 − 28 = 4 kN·m, half the clamped value wL²/8 = 8 kN·m

parts.ask: Root rotation θ_A
sol: θ_A = 1.33 mrad

parts.ask: Twist: stiffen the joint until k_θ → ∞, then loosen it until k_θ → 0. R moves between:
w: 8 kN (clamped) and 6 kN (pinned)
5 kN (5wL/16) and 8 kN (wL/2)
6 kN (3wL/8) and 16 kN (wL)
sol: k_θ → ∞: R = (wL⁴/(8EI))/(L³/(3EI)) = 3wL/8 = 6 kN
k_θ → 0: R = (wL³/(2k_θ))/(L²/k_θ) = wL/2 = 8 kN
A flexible root sends more load to the prop

problems.x: A real joint behaves as a rotational spring, and the prop reaction then lies between the clamped and pinned values, 3wL/8 and wL/2.
